newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerians urged to vote on new constitution.
newsitem.headline: Algerians urged to vote on new constitution.

text.p: Algerian army helicopters on Wednesday showered the capital of Algiers with leaflets encouraging voters to take part in a Thursday referendum that Moslem guerrillas have vowed to disrupt.
Stringent security measures have been put in place before the vote on a draft constitution that would ban Moslem fundamentalists from seeking power.

The militant Armed Islamic Group (GIA) -- the most feared of the armed Moslem movements -- has warned people not to vote, saying its guerrillas will "strike the neck" of anyone who leaves home on referendum day.

In northeastern, Berber-dominated areas a general strike started on Wednesday to protest against the proposed constitution, which activists said scorned their claim that Berber be registered as an official language.
The draft states that Arabic is the sole official language of the state.

Secular opposition Rally for Democracy and Culture (RCD), led by psychiatrist Said Saadi, claimed that the whole four million population of the region supported the strike call in schools, universities, factories and shops.
But residents said supporters of rival Socialist Forces Front (FFS) and many other people ignored the stoppage.
In Algiers, the helicopters, underlining government concern over voter turnout, showered city streets with hundreds of thousands of leaflets explaining the voting procedure, eyewitnesses said.
Algerian authorities, fearing violence, have shut schools and turned them into heavily fortified polling stations ringed by soldiers, residents said.
"Schools have been closed since three days and security forces and soldiers were put up there," said Fatiha, a housewife in Algiers's Bab el Oued, a stronghold of Moslem militants.
The government ordered a week-long closure of big markets in the cities, where thousands of paratroopers, police and paramilitary forces have deployed.
The authorities also announced a nationwide ban on truck traffic throughout the country starting on Thursday to protect against truck bomb attacks by the rebels.
"The government does not want to give any chance to armed groups," said an Algiers-based western diplomat.
More than 1,400 people have been killing in bombings in the past two years, according to a government-appointed human rights group report.
Moslem rebels earlier this week chased off telecommunications workers who wanted to fix phone lines at a polling station in the Casbah, Algiers city's heart.
"They (workers) returned the next day escorted by security forces," said a resident of the area.

Government officials and their political backers, who hope to see a high turnout of the 16.4 million potential voters to boost support for President Liamine Zeroual, made last minute calls that people endorse the constitutional reforms.
"Don't forget the years of hell and sacrifices," said Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia in a campaign rally, referring to the five-year-old civil strife.
More than 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities scrapped a general election that radical Islamists were poised to win.
Opposition leaders continued their campaign against the referendum, hoping for a low turnout to embarrass the government.
